title: Make the history gate accept squash- and rebase-merged landings
summary: `athena check --history` and the governed-content invariant assume a landing commit keeps its parent chain on main. They need the prediction commit to be an ancestor, a "no earlier landing" check, and a first-parent job.json. A squash or rebase merge rewrites or collapses those commits, so the check wrongly refuses them. I read the request as making the gate verify landings by content and records, not by commit ancestry, while still refusing unverified governed changes. Merge commits keep working.

defaults_applied.how: New gate tests for squash, rebase, and refused cases; cargo test and clippy must be clean.
Behavior criteria are checked by running cargo test, clippy and fmt --check.
The design doc §7.3/§7.4 is updated with the alternatives considered.
The change is confined to the gate's landing and prediction checks, plus docs.
The missing detail (trailers kept on squash, how rebase rewrites ids) is recovered from the code and stated as assumptions.
All changes and tests are in Rust.
The new rule is enforced by the gate and its history check, not by prose.

assumptions: A squash commit keeps the Athena-Job, Athena-Prediction and Athena-Verified-Content trailers in its message. Platforms usually build the squash message from the PR's commit messages, and the user can edit it.
The squashed or rebased commit's governed-content fingerprint equals the verified one, because the tree is the same as the PR tip's.

Rebase-merge rewrites commit ids, so Athena-Prediction may name a commit that no longer exists. The prediction check must resolve it through the records, for example the reading file already present in the parent's tree, not through git ancestry.
A squash of several Athena commits (landing plus record-only commits) into one is in scope only if the result still carries exactly one valid landing's trailers.
The weaker ancestry proof must not weaken the refusal of hand-made governed changes. Unverified squashed content stays refused.
question: Should a squash commit be required to keep the Athena-* trailers, or should Athena also recognise a squash by the PR's records, with no trailers? I assumed trailers are kept.

acceptance_criteria.text: A new gate test builds a history in which a verified landing is squash-merged onto main (one commit, parent chain rewritten, trailers kept). `cargo test -p athena-gate` shows `check_history` reporting no violations for it.
A new gate test rebase-merges a verified landing, so its commit id differs and the Athena-Prediction commit is not an ancestor by id. `cargo test -p athena-gate` shows the history check passing.

A new test shows a squash commit that changes governed content without valid landing trailers or records is still refused with Rule::Invariant, and a second landing of the same job after a squash is still refused. `cargo test -p athena-gate` passes.

Existing merge-commit tests (clean merge passes, merge with extra governed content refused) still pass. `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are all clean.

docs/design/athena-v0.md §7.3/§7.4 describes how the invariant treats merge, squash and rebase strategies and what a landing commit must carry. It names the alternatives considered and cites the code.
CHANGELOG.md has an entry, and README.md or the docs say that any of the three PR merge strategies is supported.

out_of_scope: Changing how Athena itself lands commits locally (it fast-forwards)
Configuring GitHub repository merge settings or branch protection
Changes to athena.toml, defaults.toml, or other governance files
Support for non-GitHub forges' squash message formats beyond keeping trailers
departures: The reference forecast comes from smaller jobs. This one changes security-sensitive gate logic across several functions that rely on ancestry (is_ancestor on the prediction, earlier_landing, first-parent job.json), and the design is ambiguous. I raise cost and time and lower the chance the reading and the verification pass.
